Why this compounds the siting advantage

Water permitting is not only a delay; it is a geographic filter, since permits are hardest to obtain in the stressed basins where growth is wanted. Removing the cooling-water permit burden reinforces the burner's ability to site near load in arid regions.

We make no economic or schedule claim here, and no promise about any specific jurisdiction. The defensible point is structural: the environmental effects that cooling-water permits exist to manage, withdrawal, thermal discharge, entrainment, evaporation, are absent when there is no steam cycle, so the associated regulatory processes largely do not apply.

title: Thermal Discharge & Aquatic Impact
lede: Steam plants return warmed water that lowers dissolved oxygen and stresses aquatic life; a generator with no cooling discharge avoids this entirely.
body: Once-through and some closed-loop plants return water several degrees warmer than they took it. Warmer water holds less dissolved oxygen, accelerates metabolism in fish and invertebrates, and can shift the balance of species. Sudden shutdowns cause thermal shock in organisms acclimated to the plume.
Discharge temperature limits protect dissolved oxygen levels
Mixing-zone rules limit how far the warm plume extends
Seasonal restrictions protect spawning and migration

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 260" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="260" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Thermal discharge effect</text><rect x="121" y="108" width="118" height="64" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="180" y="145" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Warm discharge</text><line x1="242" y1="140" x2="255" y2="140" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="255,135 261,140 255,145" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="261" y="108" width="118" height="64" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="320" y="145" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Lower oxygen</text><line x1="382" y1="140" x2="395" y2="140" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="395,135 401,140 395,145" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="401" y="108" width="118" height="64" rx="8" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="460" y="145" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#232C39">Aquatic stress</text><text x="320" y="236" font-size="11.5" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6B7280">Navy = process step · Gold = electricity / direct-conversion path</text></svg>
Why the burner has no thermal plume

MetroVolt rejects its small residual heat to air, not to a water body. There is no warmed cooling-water stream returned to a river or coast, so there is no thermal plume, no oxygen depletion, and no thermal-shock risk from plant trips. The impact category simply does not exist for a dry-cooled, water-light generator.

Thermal discharge is one of several aquatic impacts, intake mortality and consumptive depletion being others, that all stem from using a water body as a plant's cold sink. Removing the steam cycle removes the need for that cold sink and, with it, this whole family of impacts. The environmental benefit is a direct consequence of the water story's core mechanism.

title: Cooling-Water Intake & Entrainment
lede: Large cooling-water intakes trap fish on screens and pull eggs and larvae through the plant; a generator with no bulk intake causes neither harm.
body: Impingement: fish and larger organisms pinned against intake screens by the inflow
Entrainment: eggs, larvae, and plankton small enough to pass the screens are drawn through the plant and killed

The scale of harm rises with the volume withdrawn, so once-through plants, which withdraw enormous volumes, cause the most. Mitigation, screens, reduced intake velocity, and closed-loop conversion, reduces but does not eliminate it.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 260" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="260" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Intake harm path</text><rect x="121" y="108" width="118" height="64" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="180" y="145" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Bulk intake</text><line x1="242" y1="140" x2="255" y2="140" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="255,135 261,140 255,145" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="261" y="108" width="118" height="64" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="320" y="145" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Screen impingement</text><line x1="382" y1="140" x2="395" y2="140" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="395,135 401,140 395,145" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="401" y="108" width="118" height="64" rx="8" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="460" y="136" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#232C39">Entrainment through</text><text x="460" y="154" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#232C39">plant</text><text x="320" y="236" font-size="11.5" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6B7280">Navy = process step · Gold = electricity / direct-conversion path</text></svg>

Entrainment and impingement require a large water intake. MetroVolt has no steam condenser and therefore no bulk cooling-water intake. Its residual heat is rejected to air. Without an intake there is no screen to impinge organisms and no throughflow to entrain them.

Removing the intake removes an impact that has driven costly retrofits and litigation across the thermal fleet. It is one of the clearest, most tangible consequences of eliminating the steam cycle: no intake, no aquatic entrainment.

This benefit concerns the power plant's cooling intake specifically. A campus may still draw ordinary facility water from municipal supply. But the large ecological harm associated with power-plant cooling intakes is absent because the intake itself is absent.

title: Blowdown & Water-Treatment Waste
lede: Evaporative cooling concentrates dissolved solids, forcing periodic blowdown and treatment; a system with no evaporative loop produces neither stream.
body: In a wet cooling tower, pure water evaporates and leaves dissolved minerals behind, so the circulating water grows saltier. To keep scale and corrosion in check, operators discharge a portion, the blowdown, and replace it with fresh makeup. Chemical treatment controls scale, corrosion, and biological growth.
Concentrated blowdown water requiring discharge permits or treatment

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 260" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="260" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Evaporative waste chain</text><rect x="121" y="108" width="118" height="64" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="180" y="136" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Evaporation concentrates</text><text x="180" y="154" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">solids</text><line x1="242" y1="140" x2="255" y2="140" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="255,135 261,140 255,145" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="261" y="108" width="118" height="64" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="320" y="145" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Blowdown discharge</text><line x1="382" y1="140" x2="395" y2="140" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="395,135 401,140 395,145" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="401" y="108" width="118" height="64" rx="8" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="460" y="145" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#232C39">Treatment waste</text><text x="320" y="236" font-size="11.5" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6B7280">Navy = process step · Gold = electricity / direct-conversion path</text></svg>
Why the burner produces none of this

These streams are all consequences of evaporating water in an open recirculating loop. MetroVolt's cooling loops are closed and rejected to air; nothing evaporates to concentrate solids, so there is no blowdown, no evaporative-scaling chemistry, and no associated waste. Sealed coolant is treated once and recirculated, not continuously bled and replaced.

Beyond consuming almost no water, removing evaporative cooling removes a category of liquid waste and its permitting. The environmental profile of the water story is not only "less water in" but also "less contaminated water out."

Ordinary facility wastewater still exists at any site. The specific claim is that the power plant's evaporative-cooling waste streams, blowdown and its treatment residues, do not arise when there is no evaporative cooling loop.

title: Makeup-Water Chemistry
lede: Wet-cooled plants continuously add treated makeup water to replace evaporation and blowdown; closed dry-cooled loops need only minimal, occasional makeup.
body: An evaporative cooling system loses water constantly, to evaporation, drift, and blowdown, so it must continuously add makeup water. That makeup must be treated for hardness, pH, and biological content before it enters the loop, and the treatment scales with the volume added.
Softening or partial demineralization to limit scale
Corrosion inhibitors to protect metal surfaces
Biocides to prevent biofilm and microbial growth
Continuous monitoring of cycles of concentration

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 212" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="212" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="34" font-size="17" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Makeup-water demand (schematic)</text><text x="24" y="60" font-size="13" fill="#232C39">Wet tower</text><rect x="24" y="66" width="440" height="20" rx="4" fill="#EEF0F3"/><rect x="24" y="66" width="440" height="20" rx="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="476" y="81" font-size="12" fill="#232C39">continuous, high volume</text><text x="24" y="106" font-size="13" fill="#232C39">Hybrid</text><rect x="24" y="112" width="440" height="20" rx="4" fill="#EEF0F3"/><rect x="24" y="112" width="198" height="20" rx="4" fill="#8A93A3"/><text x="476" y="127" font-size="12" fill="#232C39">reduced</text><text x="24" y="152" font-size="13" fill="#232C39">Burner closed loop</text><rect x="24" y="158" width="440" height="20" rx="4" fill="#EEF0F3"/><rect x="24" y="158" width="17" height="20" rx="4" fill="#232C39"/><text x="476" y="173" font-size="12" fill="#232C39">occasional, minimal</text></svg>
Why the burner's makeup is minimal

A closed, dry-cooled loop does not lose water to evaporation. Its only losses are small leaks and maintenance draining, so makeup is occasional and low-volume. The loop's chemistry is set once and maintained, rather than continuously corrected for the concentrating effect of evaporation.

Minimal makeup means minimal water treatment, minimal treatment chemicals, and minimal associated waste. Each piece of the evaporative water story, consumption, makeup, treatment, and blowdown, shrinks together when the steam cycle and its cooling tower are absent.

title: Legionella & Cooling-Tower Risk
lede: Warm, aerosol-generating wet cooling towers can harbor Legionella; dry, closed cooling removes the warm-water aerosol pathway entirely.
body: Why wet towers pose a risk

Legionella bacteria thrive in warm, stagnant water and spread through inhaled aerosols. A wet cooling tower produces exactly those conditions: warm circulating water and a fine mist carried out in the airflow. Outbreaks have been traced to poorly maintained industrial and building cooling towers.
Managing the risk in wet systems
Drift eliminators to limit aerosol release

These controls reduce but do not eliminate the hazard, and they add an ongoing safety and maintenance burden, especially for towers sited near populated areas or, relevantly, near a data-center campus with staff.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 260" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="260" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Aerosol pathway</text><rect x="121" y="108" width="118" height="64" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="180" y="136" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Warm tower</text><text x="180" y="154" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">water</text><line x1="242" y1="140" x2="255" y2="140" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="255,135 261,140 255,145" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="261" y="108" width="118" height="64" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="320" y="145" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Aerosol mist</text><line x1="382" y1="140" x2="395" y2="140" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="395,135 401,140 395,145" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="401" y="108" width="118" height="64" rx="8" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="460" y="145" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#232C39">Inhalation risk</text><text x="320" y="236" font-size="11.5" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6B7280">Navy = process step · Gold = electricity / direct-conversion path</text></svg>
Why the burner's cooling is inherently safer here

MetroVolt rejects heat through closed loops to dry air heat exchangers. There is no open warm-water basin and no evaporative mist, so the Legionella aerosol pathway does not exist. The public-health risk associated with wet cooling towers is designed out, not merely managed down.

This is a secondary benefit of the water story, but a meaningful one for urban and campus siting. Removing evaporative cooling removes not only water consumption and waste streams but also the airborne-pathogen risk that comes with warm open water.

title: Water: Fission vs Thermal Fusion vs Direct Fusion
lede: Fission and any steam-cycle fusion plant both consume cooling water; only direct energy conversion breaks the link between fusion power and water.
body: It is sometimes assumed that fusion is inherently water-light. That is not true of steam-cycle fusion. A fusion plant that captures its energy as heat, boils water, and drives a turbine has the same condenser and cooling-water burden as any other steam plant. The water advantage comes from the conversion method, not from fusion itself.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 212" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="212" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="34" font-size="17" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Generation-side water by architecture (schematic)</text><text x="24" y="60" font-size="13" fill="#232C39">Fission (steam)</text><rect x="24" y="66" width="440" height="20" rx="4" fill="#EEF0F3"/><rect x="24" y="66" width="440" height="20" rx="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="476" y="81" font-size="12" fill="#232C39">condenser cooling</text><text x="24" y="106" font-size="13" fill="#232C39">Thermal fusion (steam)</text><rect x="24" y="112" width="440" height="20" rx="4" fill="#EEF0F3"/><rect x="24" y="112" width="418" height="20" rx="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="476" y="127" font-size="12" fill="#232C39">condenser cooling</text><text x="24" y="152" font-size="13" fill="#232C39">Direct-conversion fusion</text><rect x="24" y="158" width="440" height="20" rx="4" fill="#EEF0F3"/><rect x="24" y="158" width="26" height="20" rx="4" fill="#232C39"/><text x="476" y="173" font-size="12" fill="#232C39">residual only</text></svg>

A fission reactor is a heat source feeding a Rankine cycle. It rejects roughly two-thirds of its thermal output at the condenser, cooled by water like any thermal plant. Fission's water footprint is a steam-cycle footprint, not a nuclear one.
The D-3He reaction yields mostly charged particles, suited to direct conversion
Direct conversion skips the boiler, turbine, and condenser for the main output
Only the 5.44% neutron fraction and losses deposit as heat needing cooling

Compared fairly, the burner's water advantage is not "fusion beats fission" in general; a steam-cycle fusion plant would drink like a fission plant. The advantage is specifically that direct energy conversion of a charged-particle-dominant fuel removes the steam cycle. That is the distinction the water story rests on.

title: Water For Natural-Gas Plants
lede: Gas plants range from water-heavy combined-cycle steam to lower-water simple-cycle turbines, but firm gas generation still relies on a steam bottoming cycle.
body: Simple-cycle: a gas turbine alone; lower water but lower efficiency, used for peaking
Combined-cycle: a gas turbine plus a steam bottoming cycle; higher efficiency but with a condenser and its cooling water

Efficient, firm gas generation is combined-cycle, which means it carries a steam cycle and therefore a cooling-water load, typically met by wet towers. The more efficient the plant, the more it leans on that steam bottoming cycle.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 258" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="258" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="34" font-size="17" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Generation-side water for gas (schematic)</text><text x="24" y="60" font-size="13" fill="#232C39">Combined-cycle (wet)</text><rect x="24" y="66" width="440" height="20" rx="4" fill="#EEF0F3"/><rect x="24" y="66" width="440" height="20" rx="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="476" y="81" font-size="12" fill="#232C39">steam bottoming cycle</text><text x="24" y="106" font-size="13" fill="#232C39">Combined-cycle (dry)</text><rect x="24" y="112" width="440" height="20" rx="4" fill="#EEF0F3"/><rect x="24" y="112" width="88" height="20" rx="4" fill="#8A93A3"/><text x="476" y="127" font-size="12" fill="#232C39">efficiency penalty</text><text x="24" y="152" font-size="13" fill="#232C39">Simple-cycle turbine</text><rect x="24" y="158" width="440" height="20" rx="4" fill="#EEF0F3"/><rect x="24" y="158" width="35" height="20" rx="4" fill="#8A93A3"/><text x="476" y="173" font-size="12" fill="#232C39">peaking, low efficiency</text><text x="24" y="198" font-size="13" fill="#232C39">MetroVolt burner</text><rect x="24" y="204" width="440" height="20" rx="4" fill="#EEF0F3"/><rect x="24" y="204" width="17" height="20" rx="4" fill="#232C39"/><text x="476" y="219" font-size="12" fill="#232C39">no steam cycle</text></svg>

Gas is valued for firm, dispatchable power, the same property MetroVolt targets. But firm, efficient gas means combined-cycle, which means water. MetroVolt offers firmness without the steam-cycle water, addressing the same load need with a different water profile.

This page compares generation-side cooling water only, not fuel supply, emissions, or economics, which are out of scope here. The narrow, robust point is that the efficient form of firm gas generation carries a steam-cycle water burden that direct energy conversion does not.

title: Water For Coal Plants
lede: Coal generation is a steam cycle through and through, with high cooling-water consumption plus extra water for ash handling and emissions control.
body: A coal plant burns fuel to boil water and drive a steam turbine, so it carries the full condenser cooling-water load. On top of that, coal plants often use water for ash sluicing and for wet flue-gas desulfurization, adding to their total water demand beyond cooling alone.
Water uses at a coal plant
Boiler makeup and general plant water

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 212" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="212" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="34" font-size="17" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Coal-plant water uses (schematic share)</text><text x="24" y="60" font-size="13" fill="#232C39">Condenser cooling</text><rect x="24" y="66" width="440" height="20" rx="4" fill="#EEF0F3"/><rect x="24" y="66" width="440" height="20" rx="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="476" y="81" font-size="12" fill="#232C39">dominant</text><text x="24" y="106" font-size="13" fill="#232C39">Emissions control</text><rect x="24" y="112" width="440" height="20" rx="4" fill="#EEF0F3"/><rect x="24" y="112" width="79" height="20" rx="4" fill="#8A93A3"/><text x="476" y="127" font-size="12" fill="#232C39">wet scrubbers</text><text x="24" y="152" font-size="13" fill="#232C39">Ash handling</text><rect x="24" y="158" width="440" height="20" rx="4" fill="#EEF0F3"/><rect x="24" y="158" width="44" height="20" rx="4" fill="#8A93A3"/><text x="476" y="173" font-size="12" fill="#232C39">sluicing</text></svg>
Why this matters as a baseline

Coal is the high-water-intensity end of the generation spectrum and a large share of the fleet MetroVolt-style firm power could displace over time. Its water use is dominated by the same condenser cooling that direct energy conversion eliminates.

We compare only water here, not emissions or economics. Even so, the contrast is stark: a coal plant's water use begins with a large evaporative cooling load and adds more on top, while the burner's begins near zero because it has no steam cycle to cool.

title: Water For Nuclear Fission
lede: Fission plants are large steam plants and among the most water-consuming generators, because their cooling load scales with their substantial rejected heat.
body: Why fission uses so much water

A fission plant is a heat source coupled to a Rankine steam cycle. Its thermal efficiency is typically around one-third, so it rejects roughly two units of heat for every unit of electricity, all of which must be cooled. That places fission among the most water-intensive generators per unit of electricity when wet-cooled.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 166" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="166" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="34" font-size="17" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Rejected heat, schematic</text><text x="24" y="60" font-size="13" fill="#232C39">Fission electricity</text><rect x="24" y="66" width="440" height="20" rx="4" fill="#EEF0F3"/><rect x="24" y="66" width="145" height="20" rx="4" fill="#8A93A3"/><text x="476" y="81" font-size="12" fill="#232C39">useful</text><text x="24" y="106" font-size="13" fill="#232C39">Fission rejected heat</text><rect x="24" y="112" width="440" height="20" rx="4" fill="#EEF0F3"/><rect x="24" y="112" width="294" height="20" rx="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="476" y="127" font-size="12" fill="#232C39">cooling load</text></svg>
Once-through on coasts and large rivers: huge withdrawal, aquatic impacts
Dry cooling: rarely used at this scale due to efficiency and size penalties
Because fission's rejected heat is large, dry cooling is impractical, so fission plants remain tied to substantial water sources and the siting and drought constraints that come with them.

The burner's advantage over fission is not about the reaction being cleaner in some general sense; it is that the burner captures charged-particle energy directly and never builds the large steam-cycle heat-rejection load that forces fission to consume water. Only the small 5.44% neutron fraction and losses deposit as heat, which closed dry loops handle.

Fission is a proven, firm, low-carbon source; the comparison here is strictly on cooling water. On that axis, a direct-conversion generator and a fission plant sit at opposite ends because one has a steam cycle and the other does not.

title: Solar & Wind Water Footprint
lede: Wind and solar PV use very little operating water but are variable; MetroVolt aims to match their low water use while providing firm output.
body: Wind turbines and solar photovoltaics have almost no operating water footprint, since they involve no steam cycle. Their main water use is periodic panel cleaning and construction. This makes them the low-water benchmark among generators, but their output is variable and weather-dependent.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 258" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="258" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="34" font-size="17" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Operating water vs firmness (schematic)</text><text x="24" y="60" font-size="13" fill="#232C39">Wind / PV water</text><rect x="24" y="66" width="440" height="20" rx="4" fill="#EEF0F3"/><rect x="24" y="66" width="17" height="20" rx="4" fill="#232C39"/><text x="476" y="81" font-size="12" fill="#232C39">very low water</text><text x="24" y="106" font-size="13" fill="#232C39">Wind / PV firmness</text><rect x="24" y="112" width="440" height="20" rx="4" fill="#EEF0F3"/><rect x="24" y="112" width="132" height="20" rx="4" fill="#8A93A3"/><text x="476" y="127" font-size="12" fill="#232C39">variable output</text><text x="24" y="152" font-size="13" fill="#232C39">MetroVolt water</text><rect x="24" y="158" width="440" height="20" rx="4" fill="#EEF0F3"/><rect x="24" y="158" width="22" height="20" rx="4" fill="#232C39"/><text x="476" y="173" font-size="12" fill="#232C39">very low water</text><text x="24" y="198" font-size="13" fill="#232C39">MetroVolt firmness</text><rect x="24" y="204" width="440" height="20" rx="4" fill="#EEF0F3"/><rect x="24" y="204" width="418" height="20" rx="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="476" y="219" font-size="12" fill="#232C39">firm output</text></svg>

Concentrated solar power (CSP) that uses a steam cycle does consume cooling water, unlike PV. This reinforces the theme: the water burden comes from the steam cycle, not from the energy source. PV avoids it by generating electricity directly from light, much as the burner avoids it by converting charged particles directly.
Water footprint comparable to wind and PV: very low, no steam cycle
Output firm and dispatchable, unlike variable renewables
Complementary: MetroVolt can provide the firm backbone alongside variable renewables

MetroVolt is not a replacement for renewables and makes no economic claim against them. The point relevant to the water story is that firm power has historically meant a steam cycle and its water, while MetroVolt aims to deliver firmness at renewable-like water intensity by converting energy directly.

title: MetroVolt vs Conventional Water Footprint
lede: Placed on one axis, firm conventional generation clusters at high generation-side water use while MetroVolt sits with the water-light sources.
body: Ranking firm and non-firm sources by generation-side water consumption per unit of electricity produces a clear pattern. Steam-cycle sources, coal, fission, combined-cycle gas, and any thermal fusion, cluster high. Wind, PV, and direct-conversion fusion cluster near zero. The dividing line is whether a steam cycle is present.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 304" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="304" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="34" font-size="17" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Generation-side water, firm sources (schematic)</text><text x="24" y="60" font-size="13" fill="#232C39">Coal</text><rect x="24" y="66" width="440" height="20" rx="4" fill="#EEF0F3"/><rect x="24" y="66" width="440" height="20" rx="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="476" y="81" font-size="12" fill="#232C39">steam + extras</text><text x="24" y="106" font-size="13" fill="#232C39">Fission</text><rect x="24" y="112" width="440" height="20" rx="4" fill="#EEF0F3"/><rect x="24" y="112" width="404" height="20" rx="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="476" y="127" font-size="12" fill="#232C39">steam cycle</text><text x="24" y="152" font-size="13" fill="#232C39">Combined-cycle gas (wet)</text><rect x="24" y="158" width="440" height="20" rx="4" fill="#EEF0F3"/><rect x="24" y="158" width="308" height="20" rx="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="476" y="173" font-size="12" fill="#232C39">steam bottoming</text><text x="24" y="198" font-size="13" fill="#232C39">Dry-cooled thermal</text><rect x="24" y="204" width="440" height="20" rx="4" fill="#EEF0F3"/><rect x="24" y="204" width="88" height="20" rx="4" fill="#8A93A3"/><text x="476" y="219" font-size="12" fill="#232C39">efficiency penalty</text><text x="24" y="244" font-size="13" fill="#232C39">MetroVolt (DEC)</text><rect x="24" y="250" width="440" height="20" rx="4" fill="#EEF0F3"/><rect x="24" y="250" width="22" height="20" rx="4" fill="#232C39"/><text x="476" y="265" font-size="12" fill="#232C39">no steam cycle</text></svg>

MetroVolt is notable for combining two properties that rarely coexist: firm, dispatchable output and near-zero generation-side water. Conventional firm sources come with a steam cycle and its water; conventional low-water sources come with variability. Direct energy conversion is the mechanism that lets the burner have both.
Bars are schematic and directional, not certified measurements
The burner is a design-stage study; its bar reflects its architecture, not an operating record
Only generation-side cooling water is compared, not fuel-chain or facility water
On generation-side water, MetroVolt belongs with wind and solar; on firmness, it belongs with coal, gas, and fission. It occupies a corner of the map that steam-cycle physics normally keeps empty.

title: Lifecycle Water: An Honest Accounting
lede: A complete water account includes fuel supply, construction, and facility use, not just cooling; MetroVolt's advantage is clearest in operating cooling water.
body: An honest water footprint spans the whole lifecycle: extracting and processing fuel, manufacturing and constructing the plant, operating it, and decommissioning it. Cooling water is usually the dominant operating term for thermal plants, but it is not the only term.
Fuel-chain water: mining, refining, or, for the burner, producing deuterium and helium-3
Construction water: concrete, materials, and site work
Operating water: cooling plus facility and maintenance water
Where MetroVolt clearly wins, and where it does not

MetroVolt's decisive advantage is in operating cooling water, which it nearly eliminates. Construction and facility water are comparable to other plants; the burner does not claim an advantage there. Fuel-chain water for deuterium and helium-3 supply is a real term that any complete accounting must include.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 260" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="260" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Lifecycle water terms</text><rect x="51" y="108" width="118" height="64" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="110" y="145" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Fuel chain</text><line x1="172" y1="140" x2="185" y2="140" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="185,135 191,140 185,145" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="191" y="108" width="118" height="64" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="250" y="145" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Construction</text><line x1="312" y1="140" x2="325" y2="140" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="325,135 331,140 325,145" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="331" y="108" width="118" height="64" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="390" y="145" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Operating cooling</text><line x1="452" y1="140" x2="465" y2="140" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="465,135 471,140 465,145" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="471" y="108" width="118" height="64" rx="8" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="530" y="145" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#232C39">Facility</text><text x="320" y="236" font-size="11.5" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6B7280">Navy = process step · Gold = electricity / direct-conversion path</text></svg>
Why we frame it this way

Overstating the advantage across the whole lifecycle would be dishonest. The robust, defensible claim is specific: the operating cooling-water term, the one that dominates a thermal plant's footprint and drives drought and siting conflicts, is nearly removed. Other terms are ordinary.

When the burner is called water-light, it means the large, continuous, operating cooling-water draw is gone. That is the term that matters most for stressed basins and firm data-center power, and it is the term direct energy conversion actually addresses.

title: What Little Water MetroVolt Still Uses
lede: MetroVolt is water-light, not waterless: it uses ordinary facility water, occasional coolant makeup, and construction water, but no evaporative cooling.
body: Removing the steam cycle removes the dominant water draw, but a real facility still uses some water. Being precise about what remains is part of making the water story credible.
Facility water: sanitary and domestic use for staff
Coolant makeup: occasional top-up of sealed closed loops for leaks and maintenance
Water treatment: one-time and periodic conditioning of closed-loop fluids
Construction water: concrete and site work during build

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 212" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="212" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="34" font-size="17" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Where the remaining water goes (schematic)</text><text x="24" y="60" font-size="13" fill="#232C39">Facility / sanitary</text><rect x="24" y="66" width="440" height="20" rx="4" fill="#EEF0F3"/><rect x="24" y="66" width="242" height="20" rx="4" fill="#8A93A3"/><text x="476" y="81" font-size="12" fill="#232C39">staff use</text><text x="24" y="106" font-size="13" fill="#232C39">Coolant makeup</text><rect x="24" y="112" width="440" height="20" rx="4" fill="#EEF0F3"/><rect x="24" y="112" width="110" height="20" rx="4" fill="#8A93A3"/><text x="476" y="127" font-size="12" fill="#232C39">occasional</text><text x="24" y="152" font-size="13" fill="#232C39">Water treatment</text><rect x="24" y="158" width="440" height="20" rx="4" fill="#EEF0F3"/><rect x="24" y="158" width="88" height="20" rx="4" fill="#8A93A3"/><text x="476" y="173" font-size="12" fill="#232C39">periodic</text></svg>

Absent are the large, continuous terms that define a thermal plant: evaporative cooling loss, cooling-tower makeup, blowdown, and bulk intake. These do not appear because there is no steam condenser and no evaporative cooling loop.
Why the distinction is the point

"Almost no water" is exactly the right phrasing. The remaining uses are the ordinary water any building needs, not the generation-scale evaporation that stresses basins. The claim is neither zero nor exaggerated; it is that the water that scales with power output is essentially removed.

Exact residual volumes depend on final engineering, which is in simulation, with a test unit planned around 2032. The categories above, and the absence of evaporative terms, follow directly from the architecture and are robust regardless of detail.

title: Neutron Heat & Blanket Cooling
lede: The 5.44% neutron fraction deposits energy in surrounding structure and must be cooled, but this small load is carried by closed loops without evaporation.
body: The one heat load direct conversion cannot avoid

Direct energy conversion captures charged particles, but neutrons are uncharged and cannot be decelerated by an electric field. In the D-3He burner the neutron fraction is 5.44% of fusion power. Those neutrons escape the plasma and deposit their energy as heat in the surrounding structure, which must be cooled.
How the neutron heat is handled
Structure surrounding the plasma absorbs neutron energy as heat
A closed coolant loop removes that heat
The loop rejects to air, so no water is consumed by the process

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 260" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="260" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Neutron heat path</text><rect x="51" y="108" width="118" height="64" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="110" y="145" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Neutron (5.44%)</text><line x1="172" y1="140" x2="185" y2="140" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="185,135 191,140 185,145" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="191" y="108" width="118" height="64" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="250" y="145" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Structure heating</text><line x1="312" y1="140" x2="325" y2="140" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="325,135 331,140 325,145" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="331" y="108" width="118" height="64" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="390" y="145" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Closed loop</text><line x1="452" y1="140" x2="465" y2="140" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="465,135 471,140 465,145" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="471" y="108" width="118" height="64" rx="8" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="530" y="145" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#232C39">Air rejection</text><text x="320" y="236" font-size="11.5" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6B7280">Navy = process step · Gold = electricity / direct-conversion path</text></svg>
Why 5.44% keeps the water story intact

Because only 5.44% of fusion power is carried by neutrons, and because the charged-particle energy is captured directly rather than thermalized, the total heat that must be rejected is small compared with a steam plant's full rejected load. A small load can be rejected to air with a small penalty, so it does not reintroduce evaporative cooling.

This is the burner's irreducible thermal load, and the water story does not pretend otherwise. The point is one of scale: a few percent of fusion power as neutron heat is a manageable, dry-coolable load, not a steam-plant-sized rejection that would demand a cooling tower.

title: Why The Neutron Fraction Matters For Water
lede: The lower the neutron fraction, the smaller the unavoidable heat load and the easier it is to cool without water; D-3He's 5.44% keeps that load small.
body: In any fusion device, the fraction of energy carried by neutrons sets a floor on how much energy must be handled as heat, because neutrons cannot be captured by direct energy conversion. A D-T reaction carries most of its energy in neutrons; the D-3He reaction used by the burner carries only 5.44% as neutrons, leaving the rest as charged particles suited to direct conversion.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 166" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="166" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="34" font-size="17" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Energy carried as neutrons, schematic</text><text x="24" y="60" font-size="13" fill="#232C39">D-T reaction</text><rect x="24" y="66" width="440" height="20" rx="4" fill="#EEF0F3"/><rect x="24" y="66" width="440" height="20" rx="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="476" y="81" font-size="12" fill="#232C39">mostly neutrons</text><text x="24" y="106" font-size="13" fill="#232C39">D-3He burner</text><rect x="24" y="112" width="440" height="20" rx="4" fill="#EEF0F3"/><rect x="24" y="112" width="35" height="20" rx="4" fill="#8A93A3"/><text x="476" y="127" font-size="12" fill="#232C39">5.44% neutrons</text></svg>
Fewer neutrons, less heat to reject
Neutron energy becomes structural heat that must be cooled
A low neutron fraction means a small mandatory heat load
A small load is dry-rejectable, keeping water consumption near zero
The chain to the water story

The water story depends on keeping the thermal load small enough to reject to air. The choice of D-3He fuel, with its low neutron fraction, is what makes that possible: it maximizes the charged-particle energy that direct conversion can capture and minimizes the neutron energy that must be handled as heat. Fuel choice and water footprint are directly linked.

5.44% is not zero; the neutrons are real and require blanket and structural cooling, and they carry engineering implications beyond water. The water-relevant point is narrow and firm: a low neutron fraction keeps the mandatory heat load small, which is why the burner can be cooled without evaporation.
related: Water: Fission vs Thermal Fusion vs Direct Fusion

title: Closed-Loop Coolant Without Consumption
lede: A sealed coolant loop moves heat without losing water; rejecting that heat to air rather than evaporating it is what keeps consumption near zero.
body: In a closed loop, coolant circulates permanently between the heat source and a heat exchanger. It carries heat from one place to another but is not itself lost. The only losses are small leaks and maintenance draining. This is fundamentally different from an evaporative loop, where consuming water is the cooling mechanism itself.
The critical choice: reject to air, not vapor

A closed loop can reject its heat two ways: to an evaporative tower (consuming water) or to a dry air-cooled exchanger (consuming none). MetroVolt uses dry rejection because its heat loads are small enough that the efficiency penalty is minor. This combination, closed loop plus dry rejection, is what delivers near-zero water consumption.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 260" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="260" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Closed loop, dry rejection</text><rect x="51" y="108" width="118" height="64" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="110" y="145" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Heat source</text><line x1="172" y1="140" x2="185" y2="140" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="185,135 191,140 185,145" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="191" y="108" width="118" height="64" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="250" y="145" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Sealed coolant</text><line x1="312" y1="140" x2="325" y2="140" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="325,135 331,140 325,145" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="331" y="108" width="118" height="64" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="390" y="145" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Air exchanger</text><line x1="452" y1="140" x2="465" y2="140" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="465,135 471,140 465,145" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="471" y="108" width="118" height="64" rx="8" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="530" y="145" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#232C39">Ambient air</text><text x="320" y="236" font-size="11.5" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6B7280">Navy = process step · Gold = electricity / direct-conversion path</text></svg>
Why steam plants cannot do this at scale
A steam plant's rejected heat is enormous, so dry rejection costs it dearly in efficiency
The burner's residual heat is small, so dry rejection costs it little
Scale, not principle, is why one can go dry-cooled and the other struggles to

The coolant inside the burner's loops is used indefinitely, not consumed. The heat leaves as warmed air. No basin water is evaporated to make the plant run. This is the concrete mechanism behind the water story's headline: firm power with almost no water.
related: Waste-Heat Reuse For Districts & Data Centers

title: Waste-Heat Reuse For Districts & Data Centers
lede: The burner's residual heat, though small, can be delivered to district heating or campus loads instead of being rejected, using it rather than losing it.
body: Turning residual heat into a resource

Every generator produces some waste heat. The burner's is small, but rather than always rejecting it to air, a co-located facility can capture it for useful purposes. Low-grade heat is valuable for space heating, hot water, and some industrial processes.
District heating for nearby buildings or neighborhoods

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 260" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="260" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Heat reuse options</text><rect x="121" y="108" width="118" height="64" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="180" y="145" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Residual heat</text><line x1="242" y1="140" x2="255" y2="140" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="255,135 261,140 255,145" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="261" y="108" width="118" height="64" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="320" y="145" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Capture loop</text><line x1="382" y1="140" x2="395" y2="140" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="395,135 401,140 395,145" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="401" y="108" width="118" height="64" rx="8" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="460" y="136" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#232C39">District /</text><text x="460" y="154" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#232C39">campus heat</text><text x="320" y="236" font-size="11.5" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6B7280">Navy = process step · Gold = electricity / direct-conversion path</text></svg>

Waste-heat reuse fails when the generator is far from any heat user. Because MetroVolt can be sited next to a data center or within a city, its residual heat has nearby customers. The same water-light, load-adjacent siting that defines MetroVolt also makes heat reuse feasible.

Reusing residual heat reduces even the small amount that would otherwise be rejected to air, and it does so without any water. It is the opposite of a cooling tower: instead of spending water to throw heat away, the heat is delivered to a use. This deepens, rather than complicates, the water story.

Heat reuse depends on nearby demand and on grade of heat, and is an option rather than a requirement. The burner functions fully by rejecting residual heat to air. Reuse is an available enhancement that the load-adjacent, dry-cooled architecture happens to enable.

title: Dispatchability & Firmness (Qualitative)
lede: MetroVolt targets firm, dispatchable output like conventional thermal plants, but without their cooling-water dependence, so firmness does not require water.
body: A firm generator can supply power on demand, around the clock, independent of weather. Data centers, running continuous compute, need firm power. Historically, firmness has come from thermal plants, coal, gas, fission, all of which carry a steam cycle and its cooling water. Variable renewables are water-light but not firm on their own.
Conventional firm power implies a steam cycle implies cooling water
Water-light power (wind, PV) has been variable, not firm
MetroVolt aims to provide firm output with near-zero generation-side water

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 212" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="212" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="34" font-size="17" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Firmness vs generation water (schematic)</text><text x="24" y="60" font-size="13" fill="#232C39">Coal / gas / fission</text><rect x="24" y="66" width="440" height="20" rx="4" fill="#EEF0F3"/><rect x="24" y="66" width="418" height="20" rx="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="476" y="81" font-size="12" fill="#232C39">firm but water-heavy</text><text x="24" y="106" font-size="13" fill="#232C39">Wind / solar</text><rect x="24" y="112" width="440" height="20" rx="4" fill="#EEF0F3"/><rect x="24" y="112" width="132" height="20" rx="4" fill="#8A93A3"/><text x="476" y="127" font-size="12" fill="#232C39">water-light but variable</text><text x="24" y="152" font-size="13" fill="#232C39">MetroVolt</text><rect x="24" y="158" width="440" height="20" rx="4" fill="#EEF0F3"/><rect x="24" y="158" width="418" height="20" rx="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="476" y="173" font-size="12" fill="#232C39">firm and water-light</text></svg>
Why this pairing matters for data centers

A continuous compute load wants firm power and, increasingly, wants it without stressing local water. Those two wants used to conflict. MetroVolt's direct-conversion architecture aims to satisfy both, delivering steady output while consuming almost no water for generation.

Firmness here is described qualitatively; we make no economic or dispatch-cost claim, and the burner is a design-stage study with a test unit planned around 2032. The water-relevant point stands on its architecture: because firmness comes from the fusion process and direct conversion, not from a steam cycle, it does not drag a cooling-water requirement along with it.

title: Grid Siting Near Load
lede: Freed from a cooling-water source, MetroVolt can be placed where power is consumed, shortening transmission and easing interconnection.
body: Conventional firm plants are often sited where water and fuel are, then linked to demand by long transmission lines. MetroVolt's near-zero cooling-water need removes the water anchor, so it can be placed near the load it serves, a data-center campus, a city district, or an industrial site.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 260" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="260" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Siting logic compared</text><rect x="121" y="108" width="118" height="64" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="180" y="136" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Old: near</text><text x="180" y="154" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">water</text><line x1="242" y1="140" x2="255" y2="140" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="255,135 261,140 255,145" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="261" y="108" width="118" height="64" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="320" y="136" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">New: near</text><text x="320" y="154" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">load</text><line x1="382" y1="140" x2="395" y2="140" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="395,135 401,140 395,145" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="401" y="108" width="118" height="64" rx="8" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="460" y="145" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#232C39">Shorter transmission</text><text x="320" y="236" font-size="11.5" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6B7280">Navy = process step · Gold = electricity / direct-conversion path</text></svg>
Shorter transmission runs and lower line losses
Relief from congested interconnection queues in some cases
Firm local capacity that improves resilience
Opportunity to reuse residual heat nearby

None of this is possible if the generator must sit beside a river or draw a cooling-tower water supply the load site cannot provide. Removing the steam cycle removes that constraint, letting the generator and the load share a site chosen for the load. Water is the hidden variable that has kept firm generation away from load, and direct energy conversion releases it.

Siting still involves land, safety, permitting, and grid rules, and MetroVolt is not yet built. The claim is bounded: eliminating the cooling-water requirement removes one of the strongest historical reasons firm generation could not be placed next to the load it serves.

title: Reducing Transmission & Cooling Together
lede: Water-light, load-adjacent siting cuts both cooling water and transmission distance at once, because the same constraint drove plants away from load.
body: The need for a large cooling-water source pushed firm power plants toward rivers and coasts, away from where much load sits. That single constraint imposed two burdens: heavy water consumption at the plant, and long transmission to reach demand. Removing the constraint relieves both together.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 260" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="260" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Removing the water anchor</text><rect x="121" y="108" width="118" height="64" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="180" y="136" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">No cooling-water</text><text x="180" y="154" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">gate</text><line x1="242" y1="140" x2="255" y2="140" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="255,135 261,140 255,145" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="261" y="108" width="118" height="64" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="320" y="136" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Site near</text><text x="320" y="154" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">load</text><line x1="382" y1="140" x2="395" y2="140" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="395,135 401,140 395,145" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="401" y="108" width="118" height="64" rx="8" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="460" y="136" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#232C39">Less water +</text><text x="460" y="154" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#232C39">less transmission</text><text x="320" y="236" font-size="11.5" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6B7280">Navy = process step · Gold = electricity / direct-conversion path</text></svg>
No steam cycle: near-zero cooling water at the generator
Sited near load: shorter lines, lower transmission losses
Fewer new long lines needed to reach demand centers
Residual heat can serve nearby users instead of being rejected

Viewed at the system level, the burner does not just trade one resource for another; it relaxes a constraint that imposed two separate penalties. Water and distance were linked through the cooling-water anchor, and direct energy conversion cuts the anchor. The result is firm power that is both water-light and load-adjacent.

Transmission and grid planning involve many factors beyond water, and we attach no economic figures here. The specific, defensible point is that the cooling-water requirement was a shared root cause of both high plant water use and remote siting, so eliminating it addresses both at once.

title: Honest Limits: A Design-Stage Study
lede: MetroVolt's water advantage follows from its architecture, but the burner is a simulation study, not built hardware, and the water story is stated within that limit.
body: What is proven and what is designed

The water advantage rests on a proven principle: a generator with no steam cycle has no condenser cooling load. That physics is not in doubt. What is not yet demonstrated in hardware is the burner itself. It is a design-and-simulation study, with a test unit planned around 2032, perfected while the breeder (Hyperion) is built.
No hardware net-gain claim ahead of the breeder's first-of-a-kind milestone
No certified water figures; comparisons here are schematic and directional
No economic claim of any kind attached to the water advantage
No assertion that the burner uses zero water, only almost none for generation

Even at the design stage, the water story's core is firm because it is architectural. Remove the steam cycle and you remove steam-cycle water; that conclusion does not depend on the final component detail, only on using direct energy conversion for the dominant output. The frozen neutron fraction of 5.44% bounds the mandatory heat load that remains.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 260" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="260" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="32" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Confidence structure</text><rect x="121" y="108" width="118" height="64" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="180" y="145" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Proven physics</text><line x1="242" y1="140" x2="255" y2="140" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="255,135 261,140 255,145" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="261" y="108" width="118" height="64" rx="8" fill="#232C39"/><text x="320" y="145" font-size="13" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#fff">Design-stage machine</text><line x1="382" y1="140" x2="395" y2="140" stroke="#D4AD5C" stroke-width="2.5"/><polygon points="395,135 401,140 395,145" fill="#D4AD5C"/><rect x="401" y="108" width="118" height="64" rx="8" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="460" y="136" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#232C39">Bounded water</text><text x="460" y="154" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle" fill="#232C39">claim</text><text x="320" y="236" font-size="11.5" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6B7280">Navy = process step · Gold = electricity / direct-conversion path</text></svg>

A credible water story is a bounded one. Overclaiming, zero water, guaranteed performance, built-and-proven, would undermine the genuine, defensible point. MetroVolt's honest claim is narrow and strong: as a direct-conversion generator, its architecture removes the largest reason power plants consume water, and that will hold when it is built.

title: The Water Story: Summary Scorecard
lede: One page, graded on the same ruler: how MetroVolt compares to conventional firm generation on every water dimension that matters.
body: The whole argument in one view

The water story reduces to a single mechanism with many consequences: direct energy conversion removes the steam cycle, and everything that steam-cycle cooling implies goes with it. This page collects the dimensions and grades them side by side.

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 212" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" style="max-width:640px;display:block;margin:1rem auto;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="212" rx="10" fill="#fff" stroke="#232C39" stroke-width="1"/><text x="24" y="34" font-size="17" font-weight="700" fill="#232C39">Generation-side water, final comparison (schematic)</text><text x="24" y="60" font-size="13" fill="#232C39">Wet steam plant</text><rect x="24" y="66" width="440" height="20" rx="4" fill="#EEF0F3"/><rect x="24" y="66" width="440" height="20" rx="4" fill="#D4AD5C"/><text x="476" y="81" font-size="12" fill="#232C39">condenser cooling</text><text x="24" y="106" font-size="13" fill="#232C39">Dry-cooled steam plant</text><rect x="24" y="112" width="440" height="20" rx="4" fill="#EEF0F3"/><rect x="24" y="112" width="88" height="20" rx="4" fill="#8A93A3"/><text x="476" y="127" font-size="12" fill="#232C39">efficiency penalty</text><text x="24" y="152" font-size="13" fill="#232C39">MetroVolt burner</text><rect x="24" y="158" width="440" height="20" rx="4" fill="#EEF0F3"/><rect x="24" y="158" width="22" height="20" rx="4" fill="#232C39"/><text x="476" y="173" font-size="12" fill="#232C39">residual only</text></svg>

On every water dimension tied to the steam cycle, MetroVolt scores near the floor, while matching conventional plants on firmness. The one row where the burner still carries a load, residual cooling, is handled by closed loops rejected to air, not by evaporation.
The advantage is architectural: no steam cycle, no steam-cycle water
It is stated at design stage, with a test unit planned around 2032
It is water-specific: no economic claims are made here
"Almost no water" is precise, not zero, and not exaggerated

Read together, the section makes one honest, defensible case: firm power for data centers and cities can be delivered with almost no water when the steam cycle is replaced by direct energy conversion.

title: Glossary: Water & Cooling Terms
lede: Plain definitions of the water and cooling terms used across the MetroVolt water story, from blowdown to withdrawal.
body: Cold sink: the reservoir that receives a heat engine's rejected heat
Condenser: the component that condenses turbine exhaust steam, the main cooling load in a steam plant
Rankine cycle: the steam cycle of boiler, turbine, condenser, and pump
Heat rejection: moving waste heat from a plant to the environment
Latent heat: energy absorbed when water evaporates, the basis of wet cooling
Once-through cooling: draws water, passes it once, returns it warmer
Wet cooling tower: rejects heat by evaporating recirculating water
Dry cooling (ACC): rejects heat to air with no evaporation
Hybrid cooling: blends wet and dry to balance water and efficiency
Closed loop: sealed coolant that carries heat without being consumed
Withdrawal: water removed from a source, some returned
Makeup water: water added to replace evaporation and blowdown
Blowdown: concentrated water discharged from an evaporative loop
WUE: water usage effectiveness, litres consumed per unit of IT energy
PUE: power usage effectiveness, total facility power per unit of IT power
Impingement: organisms trapped against an intake screen
Entrainment: small organisms drawn through the plant
Thermal discharge: warmed cooling water returned to a water body
Direct energy conversion (DEC): capturing charged-particle energy as electricity without a heat engine
Neutron fraction: share of fusion power carried by neutrons; 5.44% for the D-3He burner
Tandem mirror: the burner's magnetic confinement geometry, 26.49 T plug and 17 T throat
Residual heat: the small heat load, from neutrons and losses, that the burner still must cool
